To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the inhibition of irrelevant category-response mappings is a key factor in explaining n – 2 costs in the context of a relative-judgment task.
the n – 2 cost is reduced when irrelevant mappings are held constant.
the n – 2 switch cost is larger than the n – 1 repetition cost, and the n – 3 repetition cost is larger than n – 4.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of inhibition in task-switching and the mechanisms involved in task-set inhibition.
the cognitive mechanisms that support the flexible use of task-relevant information and the suppression of task-irrelevant information in a task environment.
the cognitive control mechanisms that underlie task-set reconfiguration.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results support the hypothesis of task-set inhibition, and that the n -2 repetition cost reflects inhibition of the irrelevant category-response mappings involved in response generation.
the inhibition of irrelevant category-response mappings is a key factor that contributes to the n -2 repetition cost effect.
inhibition of task sets is a general mechanism that is involved in the control of task switching.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
inhibition is not a unitary process but rather is sensitive to the specific demands of the task.
the n – 2 cost reflects inhibition of irrelevant category-response mappings, which are not inhibited when the response set is the same.
inhibition of task-irrelevant category–response mappings is involved in task-set inhibition, and that this inhibition is a key component of the n – 2 cost effect.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the n – 2 cost is a task-switching phenomenon, which can be used to study the mechanisms involved in switching between tasks.
n – 2 costs can be observed in situations in which all stimuli are from the same category.
the inhibition hypothesis can be used to explain divergent findings from previous studies.
